method_card.title: How to Find HCF, LCM and Prime Factorisations
method_card.content:
Prime factorisation writes a number as a product of primes, e.g. \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\). Use a factor tree and record it in index form.

HCF (Highest Common Factor): factorise both numbers, then multiply the shared primes at their lowest power.

LCM (Lowest Common Multiple): multiply every prime that appears in either number at its highest power.

Quick check: HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.
method_card.example:
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36

Step 1: \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\) and \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\)

Step 2, HCF: Shared primes: 2 and 3. Lowest powers: \(2^2\) and \(3^1\). HCF = \(2^2 \times 3 = 4 \times 3 = 12\)

Step 3, LCM: All primes: 2 and 3. Highest powers: \(2^3\) and \(3^2\). LCM = \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 8 \times 9 = 72\)

Check: \(12 \times 72 = 864 = 24 \times 36\) ✔

steps: For three numbers, factorise all of them and take the highest power of every prime that appears in any of them.
Use the shortcut HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers to find a missing number.
To turn index form into a whole number, work out each power first (\(2^3 = 8\), not \(2 \times 3\)) then multiply.
gold.title: Gold: multi-number LCM and the HCF × LCM rule

steps: Prime factorise with a factor tree: keep splitting until every end is a prime, then write it in index form, e.g. \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\).
HCF (Highest Common Factor) is the biggest number that divides into both. LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) is the smallest number both divide into.
For small numbers, spot the HCF by testing shared factors, and the LCM by listing multiples until they first match.
bronze.title: Bronze: prime factors and simple HCF/LCM

steps.label: Highest powers
steps.content: Highest power of 2 is \(2^3 = 8\); highest power of 3 is 3.

steps: Write bigger numbers as products of primes in index form, e.g. \(180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\).
HCF: multiply the shared primes at their lowest power. LCM: multiply every prime that appears at its highest power.
Read the question carefully: HCF gives a factor (smaller), LCM gives a multiple (larger). Do not just multiply the two numbers unless they share no factors.
silver.title: Silver: index notation and choosing HCF vs LCM

gold.hint: Write both as products of primes: 48 = 2⁴ × 3, 180 = 2² × 3² × 5, then take shared lowest powers.
gold.display: Find the HCF and LCM of \(48\) and \(180\). What is the HCF?

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(48 = 2^4 \times 3\) and \(180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\). Shared primes: 2 and 3.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 2, the lower of 4 and 2, is
guided_steps.hint: 48 has four 2s, 180 has two. Take the lower.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 3, the lower of 1 and 2, is
guided_steps.hint: 48 has one 3, 180 has two. Take the lower.

guided_steps.say: So HCF = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3.

guided_steps.done: 12 divides both 48 and 180 exactly, so the HCF is 12.

misconceptions.message: 720 is the LCM. The HCF = 12.

gold.hint: Use HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.
gold.display: The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their LCM is 120. One number is 24. Find the other.

guided_steps.say: Use the rule HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.
That product equals the two numbers multiplied: 24 × other = 720.

guided_steps.done: 24 × 30 = 720 = 6 × 120, so the other number is 30.

misconceptions.message: HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers. So 6 × 120 = 24 × other, giving other = 30.
That treats the LCM as the product of the numbers. It is not: HCF × LCM = 6 × 120 = 720 = 24 × other, so other = 720 ÷ 24 = 30.

gold.hint: Work out each prime power first, then multiply.

guided_steps.say: Work out each prime power first, then multiply. Remember 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, not 2 × 3.
The middle term is just 3, so the product is 8 × 3 × 25.

guided_steps.done: 600 ÷ 25 = 24 = 8 × 3, which matches 2³ × 3, so 600 is right.

misconceptions.message: You multiplied the base by the index instead of raising to a power. 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 (not 2 × 3 = 6), and 5² means 5 × 5 = 25. So 8 × 3 × 25 = 600.

gold.hint: Factorise all three, then take the highest power of each prime.

guided_steps.say: Three numbers now. Factorise each: \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\). LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears: 2², 3², 5.

guided_steps.hint: 12 has the most 2s: two of them, 2² = 4.

guided_steps.say: The highest power of 5 is just 5 (only 30 has it). So LCM = 4 × 9 × 5.

guided_steps.done: 180 divides by 12, 18 and 30, and is the smallest such number, so LCM = 180.

misconceptions.message: Use all three numbers. Factorise each and take the highest power of every prime that appears: 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.
Do not just multiply all three (12 × 18 × 30 = 6480). Use prime factorisations with highest powers: 180.

gold.hint: Find the LCM of 12 and 18, which gives the number of minutes.
gold.display: Two buses leave a station at 9 am. Bus A runs every 12 minutes, Bus B every 18 minutes. How many minutes after 9 am do they next leave together?

guided_steps.say: They leave together again after the Lowest Common Multiple of 12 and 18 minutes.
Primes: \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\) and \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\). Highest powers: 2² and 3².

guided_steps.done: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 36 ÷ 18 = 2, both whole, so they next leave together after 36 minutes.

misconceptions.message: 6 is the HCF. You need the LCM, the first time they coincide: LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.
12 × 18 = 216, but the LCM is 36. They next leave together after 36 minutes.

bronze.hint: Prime factorise 36, then add the two powers.
bronze.display: Write \(36\) as a product of prime factors. Give the answer as \(2^a \times 3^b\). What is \(a + b\)?

guided_steps.say: Build 36 from its prime building blocks. Split off the 2s first, then the 3s.

guided_steps.hint: Halve 18. After this 9 is odd, so no more 2s divide in.

guided_steps.say: So 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = \(2^2 \times 3^2\). That gives a = 2 and b = 2.

guided_steps.done: That rebuilds 36, so a + b = 4 is right.

misconceptions.message: Make sure every factor is prime. 36 = 4 × 9 is not fully factorised, keep splitting.

bronze.hint: Factorise both, then multiply the shared primes at their lowest power.

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\) and \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\). HCF multiplies the shared primes at their lowest power.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 2, the lower of 2 and 1, is
guided_steps.hint: 12 has two 2s, 18 has one. Take the lower.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 3, the lower of 1 and 2, is
guided_steps.hint: 12 has one 3, 18 has two. Take the lower.

guided_steps.say: So HCF = 2 × 3.

guided_steps.done: 6 divides both 12 and 18 exactly, so HCF = 6.

misconceptions.message: 36 is the LCM. The HCF is the largest number that divides into both 12 and 18, which is 6.
3 is a common factor but not the highest. Both 12 and 18 also divide by 6.

bronze.hint: Factorise both, then multiply each prime at its highest power.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(6 = 2 \times 3\) and \(10 = 2 \times 5\). LCM uses every prime that appears, each at its highest power: here 2, 3 and 5.

guided_steps.done: 30 divides by both 6 and 10 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 30.

misconceptions.message: 2 is the HCF, not the LCM. The LCM is the smallest number both 6 and 10 divide into: 30.
6 × 10 = 60 is a common multiple, but not the lowest. LCM = 30.

bronze.hint: The only prime 15 and 25 share is 5.

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(15 = 3 \times 5\) and \(25 = 5^2\). The only shared prime is 5, taken at the lower power.
That is the lower count, so the HCF is one 5.

guided_steps.done: 5 divides both 15 and 25 exactly and nothing bigger does, so HCF = 5.

misconceptions.message: 75 is the LCM. The HCF is the biggest number that goes into both 15 and 25, which is 5.
1 is always a common factor but not the highest here. Both numbers divide by 5.

bronze.hint: Take the highest power of each prime: 2² from 4, and 3 from 6.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(4 = 2^2\) and \(6 = 2 \times 3\). LCM takes the highest power of each prime: 2² from 4, and 3 from 6.

guided_steps.pre: Work out the highest power of 2: 2² =

guided_steps.done: 12 divides by both 4 and 6 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 12.

misconceptions.message: 4 × 6 = 24, but 12 is a smaller common multiple. Use prime factors.
2 is the HCF. The LCM is the smallest number both 4 and 6 divide into: 12.

bronze.hint: Factorise 30, then count the distinct primes.
bronze.display: List the prime factors of \(30\). How many different prime factors are there?

guided_steps.say: Break 30 into primes with a factor tree.
5 is prime, so 30 = 2 × 3 × 5. Now count the DIFFERENT primes: 2, 3 and 5.

guided_steps.done: That rebuilds 30 from three different primes, so the answer is 3.

misconceptions.message: 8 is the total number of factors of 30. The question asks for different PRIME factors: 2, 3 and 5, so 3.
Count only prime factors: 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, three of them.

bronze.hint: Multiply the shared primes at their lowest power.

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\) and \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\). Shared primes: 2 and 5.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 2, the lower of 2 and 1, is
guided_steps.hint: 20 has two 2s, 30 has one. Take the lower.

guided_steps.say: They also share one 5 each. So HCF = 2 × 5.

guided_steps.done: 10 divides both 20 and 30 exactly, so HCF = 10.

misconceptions.message: 60 is the LCM. For the HCF, multiply the shared primes at their lowest power: 2 × 5 = 10.
5 is a common factor but 10 is higher, since both 20 and 30 divide by 10.

bronze.hint: Highest power of 2 is 2³; then bring in the 3.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(8 = 2^3\) and \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\). Highest power of 2 is 2³ = 8; then bring in the 3.

guided_steps.done: 24 divides by both 8 and 12 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 24.

misconceptions.message: 8 × 12 = 96, but the LCM is smaller. Use primes: 8 = 2³, 12 = 2² × 3, so LCM = 2³ × 3 = 24.
4 is the HCF. The LCM is 24.

silver.hint: Peel off 2s from 180 until an odd number is left, then count them.
silver.display: Write \(180\) as a product of prime factors. How many 2s appear?

guided_steps.say: Factor 180 down to primes. Peel off 2s first.

guided_steps.hint: Halve 90. After this 45 is odd, so no more 2s.

guided_steps.say: 45 is odd, so the 2s stop here. 180 = 2 × 2 × 45 = \(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\).

guided_steps.done: 180 = 2² × 45, so exactly two 2s appear.

misconceptions.message: 5 counts every prime factor. The question asks only how many 2s: 180 = 2² × 3² × 5, so two 2s.
180 = 2² × 3² × 5. The power of 2 is 2, so two 2s appear.

silver.hint: Shared primes at their lowest power: 2² and 3.

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\) and \(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\). Shared primes: 2 and 3.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 2, the lower of 2 and 2, is
guided_steps.hint: Both have two 2s. Take that count, 2.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 3, the lower of 2 and 1, is
guided_steps.hint: 36 has two 3s, 84 has one. Take the lower.

guided_steps.say: So HCF = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3.

guided_steps.done: 12 divides both 36 and 84 exactly, so HCF = 12.

misconceptions.message: 252 is the LCM. For the HCF, use the lowest power of the shared primes.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(15 = 3 \times 5\) and \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\). Highest powers: 2² from 20, 3 from 15, 5 from either.

guided_steps.done: 60 divides by both 15 and 20 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 60.

misconceptions.message: 5 is the HCF, not the LCM.

silver.hint: Shared primes at their lowest power: 2³ and 3.

guided_steps.say: Prime factors: \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\) and \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\). Shared primes: 2 and 3.

guided_steps.pre: Shared power of 2, the lower of 3 and 3, is
Shared power of 3, the lower of 2 and 1, is
guided_steps.hint: 72 has two 3s, 120 has one. Take the lower.

guided_steps.say: So HCF = 2³ × 3 = 8 × 3.

guided_steps.done: 24 divides both 72 and 120 exactly, so HCF = 24.

misconceptions.message: 360 is the LCM. The HCF uses the lowest powers of the shared primes.

silver.hint: Highest power of each prime: 2³ from 24 and 3² from 18.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\) and \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\). Highest powers: 2³ from 24, 3² from 18.

guided_steps.done: 72 divides by both 18 and 24 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 72.

misconceptions.message: 18 × 24 = 432, but the LCM is smaller. 18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3, so LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72.
6 is the HCF. For the LCM, use the highest power of each prime: 2³ from 24 and 3² from 18, giving 8 × 9 = 72.

silver.display: Write \(1080\) as a product of prime factors. What is the sum of all the index values?

guided_steps.say: Factor 1080 into primes. Peel off 2s, then 3s, then what is left.

guided_steps.hint: Halve 270. 135 is odd, so the 2s stop: three 2s.

guided_steps.say: 135 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5, so 1080 = \(2^3 \times 3^3 \times 5^1\). The indices are 3, 3 and 1.

guided_steps.done: 2³ × 3³ × 5 rebuilds 1080, so the index sum is 7.

misconceptions.message: 1080 = 2³ × 3³ × 5¹. Sum of indices: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
Add the index values, do not multiply them: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 (multiplying gives 9).

silver.hint: Highest power of each prime: 3² from 9 and 5 from 15.

guided_steps.say: Primes: \(9 = 3^2\) and \(15 = 3 \times 5\). Highest powers: 3² from 9, and 5 from 15.

guided_steps.done: 45 divides by both 9 and 15 and is the smallest that does, so LCM = 45.

misconceptions.message: 3 is the HCF. The LCM = 45.
